Confirm what support is available and how preferences can be recorded. - **What should you clarify before leaving hospital?:** Ask your treating team to clarify follow-up appointments, medicine changes, personalised warning signs and after-hours contacts. Discuss how interpreter needs and relevant cultural preferences can be passed to follow-up services. ## What happens in a mental health hospital? If someone is in immediate danger, call 000, as Lifeline advises. For urgent care, the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing directs people to their local hospital emergency department. Lifeline also provides crisis support on 13 11 14, available 24/7. If a mental health hospital admission is being considered, ask the team to explain what assessment will involve, how treatment decisions will be made and how they will plan for care after you leave. Confirm the arrangements at the hospital involved rather than expecting a fixed routine, length of stay or outcome. You may also have questions about speaking in your preferred language, involving family, managing work or keeping information private. You can raise these alongside questions about treatment and explain which concerns matter most to you. Browsing community therapist profiles is a separate option for routine support, not a way to obtain urgent care or hospital admission. ## How admission can happen If you need urgent care, go to the emergency department at your local hospital. The Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing also lists your state or territory’s Mental Health Crisis Assessment and Treatment Team as a source of help. Its mental health overview provides these urgent-help routes, rather than a complete guide to admission: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. For a possible planned admission, ask your GP, psychiatrist or current treating service who to contact and what the local process involves. Useful questions include: “What referral or assessment is needed?”, “Who decides whether inpatient care is appropriate?” and “What happens if admission is not recommended or a bed is unavailable?” Ask the hospital to explain its requirements rather than treating a referral as confirmation of a place. If you are considering private care, ask the hospital and your insurer separately about cover and potential costs. You can raise communication needs before arriving: “Can my preferred language, dialect or accessibility needs be recorded?” and “How can I request a qualified interpreter for the assessment?” You do not need to wait until a treatment discussion to say what would help you understand and participate. ![Back view of a person in a dark quilted jacket with a shoulder strap, near glass doors and a wheeled stretcher.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU0A4049LNR4%2FGshah810%2FTalaThrive-marketing-site%2Fimages%2Finline-2a483aaa-5812-4051-88c1-1cca679d8035.jpg?alt=media&token=f982cbeb-0323-4aa5-8e2f-67e509eb5ca3) ## Voluntary and involuntary care and your rights Western Australia’s official guidance explains that involuntary treatment can take place in hospital or in the community. Ask about admission status and consent to each proposed treatment separately, rather than assuming that your status answers every question about treatment choices. Each state and territory has its own mental health legislation, as the Australian Government explains: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. Ask the team: “What is my current legal status?”, “What does that mean for treatment and leaving hospital?” and “Which rules apply here?” You can also ask: “How can I request a review?” and “Who can explain my rights independently?” In Western Australia, Think Mental Health’s laws and rights page describes the roles of the Mental Health Advocacy Service and Mental Health Tribunal: https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/. In Victoria, the health department’s Act guide explains supported decision making and non-legal advocacy for people receiving compulsory mental health services: https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act. These resources describe their own jurisdictions, not nationwide rules. Elsewhere, ask staff for the relevant official health-department, tribunal or advocacy resource. If the explanation is difficult to follow, you could say: “Please explain my status and choices in a language and format I understand. Can you arrange an interpreter or help me find suitable information?” Victoria’s official guide includes translated and easy-read resources. Ask what is available where you are. > **Check the rules that apply to you** > > Ask staff to explain which state or territory rules apply to your circumstances. This guide is not individual legal advice. ## A preparation checklist for you and your family Follow the hospital’s own admission instructions rather than treating this as a universal packing list. Use these prompts to ask what you need and what can wait. Packing or paperwork should not delay urgent help: the Australian Government Department of Health advises going to your local hospital’s emergency department if you need urgent care. Ask which documents and belongings to bring. Questions might include: “Do I need identification, Medicare or insurance details?” and “What clothing and toiletries are permitted?” Consider keeping important contact numbers somewhere you can access them without your phone. Confirm the hospital’s instructions before bringing items you are unsure about. For health information, ask what the team needs about your current medicines, doses and allergies. If available, gather contact details for your treating clinicians and any existing care documents. Ask how to bring and hand over medicines, rather than assuming you should keep them with you or manage them yourself during admission. Consider whether someone you trust could help with dependants, household tasks or contacting work or study. Discuss what you want that person to say and what you would prefer to keep private. If you need documentation for an absence, ask the hospital what it can provide and check what your workplace or education provider requires. Check local arrangements for phones, chargers, valuables, visiting and any restrictions on belongings. Raise food needs, religious items or practices that matter to you, and ask what arrangements are possible. Check with the hospital and, if applicable, your insurer whether there are any excess, gap or out-of-pocket charges. ## Assessment, daily routines and treatment planning ### Assessment when you arrive Ask the team to explain what your assessment will involve and what information they need from you. You could ask, “Who should I tell about my current concerns, physical health, medicines or anything that makes it difficult to feel safe?” If you need language or communication support, ask how this can be arranged for the assessment. You can also raise what matters to you beyond your symptoms: “Could we discuss how my language, faith, previous experiences or family circumstances affect this plan?” ### Daily care and treatment decisions Ask for an explanation of the ward’s daily arrangements, including meals, rest, any activities and opportunities to speak with the treating team. Confirm the rules about leave rather than relying on another person’s hospital experience. A useful starting question is, “Who can I speak to if I need help or have a concern between planned discussions?” For treatment planning, ask who is coordinating your care, what each proposed treatment is intended to address, what alternatives exist and how your preferences will be considered. You can also ask the team to explain which decisions require your consent and how your current legal status affects those decisions. If medicine is proposed, ask the prescriber or pharmacist about its purpose, expected benefits, possible side effects and when to seek help. Healthdirect’s medicines directory includes general information about antidepressants, antipsychotic medicines and lithium: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. Use it to prepare questions, not as individual prescribing advice or a reason to change your medicine yourself. ## Ask for support that reflects your language and culture Tell the team which language and dialect you prefer for conversations about your care. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ community mental health principles emphasise considering multicultural perspectives, but they do not establish what interpreter support a particular hospital offers. Ask: “Could you arrange a qualified health interpreter in my preferred language and dialect for assessment, treatment discussions and discharge?” Follow up by asking what is available, how interpretation will happen and how confidentiality is handled. If you would prefer not to have relatives interpret, you could say: “I would like to speak with the team without relatives interpreting. What arrangements are available?” Ask about a private conversation and what will happen if an interpreter is unavailable for a planned discussion. These are requests, not promises about a particular interpreter, appointment time or type of service. Choose which parts of your identity and daily life you want the team to understand. That might include prayer, food needs, modesty, a preference about a clinician’s gender, or having no religious affiliation. Experiences of racism or concerns about stigma may also be relevant to what you want to discuss. You do not need to raise every topic, and someone from the same background may have different preferences. You can ask: “How can we record what matters to me in my care plan, and revisit it if my needs change?” If fasting or another religious practice raises questions about treatment, ask the treating team to discuss it with you before making any changes to medicines. ## How family can help while respecting privacy Tell the treating team whom you would like involved, which conversations you want them to attend and what you would prefer to discuss privately. Your preferred support person might be a relative, chosen family member or trusted friend. Be specific about what feels helpful to you, rather than leaving others to assume that family members share your cultural, religious or treatment preferences. You could say: “Please record who I want involved and what I am comfortable sharing. Can you explain when the law may allow or require information to be shared without my consent?” Ask how to update those preferences and what they mean in your circumstances. Privacy preferences do not necessarily prevent every disclosure. For advice about consent, confidentiality exceptions or any formal carer or nominated-person role, ask the team to explain the applicable state or territory rules and provide the relevant official patient information. If you are supporting someone in hospital, start by asking what they want from you. Check before visiting, offer help with responsibilities they agree to hand over, or write down questions they want to raise with the team. Listen without pressing them to explain more than they wish to share. Your perspective may be valuable, but it may differ from theirs. If you have concerns to pass on, ask the team how to provide that information, how it will be recorded and who may see it. Also ask what the team can share with you in return. Do not assume that providing information means you will receive details about the person’s care, or that what you tell staff will remain confidential from them. ## A discharge checklist for the next stage of care Before you leave hospital, use these questions to discuss what happens next with your treating team. They are conversation prompts, not a standard discharge protocol or a promise that particular services or appointments will be available. ### Confirm follow-up and who is responsible Ask: “Which appointments and referrals are confirmed, which still need arranging, and who is responsible for each?” Clarify whom to contact if an appointment is unavailable or you cannot attend. Discuss how relevant information will reach your GP, community mental health team or therapist, and ask what consent arrangements apply. If something is still pending, ask what support you should use while waiting. ### Clarify medicines and prescription arrangements If medicines are part of your plan, ask for a clear current list and an explanation of any changes. Questions for the prescriber or pharmacist include: “What is each medicine for? How should I take it? What side effects need attention, and whom should I contact?” Check how to obtain your supply and future prescriptions. For general background, healthdirect’s medicines directory covers benefits, side effects and safe use of a range of medicines: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. It does not replace advice about your own prescription. ### Separate warning signs from emergency actions Ask the team to discuss warning signs relevant to you and agree on what to do if they appear. Clarify which concerns should prompt contact with your treating service, which need urgent assessment, and what clinical contact is available after hours. Keep these details somewhere you can find them easily. If someone is in immediate danger, call 000. Lifeline provides crisis support on 13 11 14 at any time, but this is not an emergency response service: https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114. For urgent care, go to your local hospital emergency department, as advised by the Australian Government Department of Health: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. ### Carry your practical and cultural preferences forward Discuss any work or study concerns, the support you would welcome from chosen family or friends, and what you want shared with them. Ask how interpreter needs and relevant cultural or religious preferences can be passed on to follow-up services. You might ask: “How will my next therapist understand my cultural context and coordinate with my treating team?” ## Finding a community therapist who understands your context For ongoing therapy after discharge, ask your treating team how a new therapist could fit into your care plan. Browsing profiles should not replace arranged psychiatric, medication or community follow-up, or be used to seek urgent care. When speaking with a prospective therapist, start with what matters to you rather than feeling you need to explain your whole background. You might ask: “What experience do you have supporting people with my concerns?” and “How do you make room for culture, faith or language in therapy?” If relevant, ask whether you can use your preferred language and discuss family expectations or experiences of discrimination without assumptions about your community. A shared background may be a meaningful preference, but it does not guarantee understanding or a good therapeutic fit. Questions such as “How do you work with someone whose background differs from yours?” and “What would you do if I felt misunderstood?” can help you discuss how the therapist approaches differences and responds to feedback. These are conversation prompts, not a validated way to assess a practitioner. Before booking, ask about qualifications, experience with the support recommended at discharge, availability and fees. You can also ask: “With my consent, how would you coordinate with my GP or treating team, and what information would you share?” A profile is a starting point for that discussion, not confirmation that a practitioner can meet every post-hospital need. ## Your next conversation with the care team Before your next conversation with the care team, write down what you need explained, whom you would like involved and what support you need after discharge. Choose the concerns that matter to you, rather than feeling you have to cover everything at once. Ask the team to clarify anything that remains uncertain, including who to contact about unanswered questions or gaps in follow-up. If you are considering a community therapist, ask how that support would fit alongside your agreed care plan. ![A mug, pen, spiral notebook and closed laptop sit on a wooden table near a window, with leafy plants and a wooden chair nearby.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU0A4049LNR4%2FGshah810%2FTalaThrive-marketing-site%2Fimages%2Finline-fb769e4f-74ad-4e48-a62c-17c5e4addd69.jpg?alt=media&token=c079322d-268f-4e67-b893-6551367552a2) ## Next Step **Sign up** Browse therapists that match your cultural background [Browse therapists that understand your cultural background](https://app.talathrive.com/login) ## References - [Lifeline crisis support - 13 11 14](https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114) - [Medicines information | healthdirect](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines) - [What we're doing about mental health | Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en) - [Mental health for the community | RANZCP](https://www.ranzcp.org/clinical-guidelines-publications/clinical-guidelines-publications-library/mental-health-for-the-community) - [Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 | health.vic.gov.au](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act) - [Mental Health Laws And Rights | Think Mental Health](https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/) - [Bruce Private Hospital | Hyson Green mental health | Calvary Health Care](https://www.calvarycare.org.au/hospitals/calvary-bruce-private-hospital/services-and-clinics-1/hyson-green-mental-health) - [Tala Thrive | Culturally matched therapy & coaching](https://talathrive.com/)

sections.heading: What happens in a mental health hospital?
paragraphs: If someone is in immediate danger, call 000, as Lifeline advises. For urgent care, the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing directs people to their local hospital emergency department. Lifeline also provides crisis support on 13 11 14, available 24/7.

If a mental health hospital admission is being considered, ask the team to explain what assessment will involve, how treatment decisions will be made and how they will plan for care after you leave. Confirm the arrangements at the hospital involved rather than expecting a fixed routine, length of stay or outcome.

You may also have questions about speaking in your preferred language, involving family, managing work or keeping information private. You can raise these alongside questions about treatment and explain which concerns matter most to you. Browsing community therapist profiles is a separate option for routine support, not a way to obtain urgent care or hospital admission.

Confirm the arrangements at the hospital involved rather than expecting a fixed routine, length of stay or outcome.

You may also have questions about speaking in your preferred language, involving family, managing work or keeping information private. You can raise these alongside questions about treatment and explain which concerns matter most to you. Browsing community therapist profiles is a separate option for routine support, not a way to obtain urgent care or hospital admission.

sections.heading: How admission can happen
paragraphs: If you need urgent care, go to the emergency department at your local hospital. The Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing also lists your state or territory’s Mental Health Crisis Assessment and Treatment Team as a source of help. Its mental health overview provides these urgent-help routes, rather than a complete guide to admission: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en.

For a possible planned admission, ask your GP, psychiatrist or current treating service who to contact and what the local process involves. Useful questions include: “What referral or assessment is needed?”, “Who decides whether inpatient care is appropriate?” and “What happens if admission is not recommended or a bed is unavailable?”

Ask the hospital to explain its requirements rather than treating a referral as confirmation of a place. If you are considering private care, ask the hospital and your insurer separately about cover and potential costs.

You can raise communication needs before arriving: “Can my preferred language, dialect or accessibility needs be recorded?” and “How can I request a qualified interpreter for the assessment?” You do not need to wait until a treatment discussion to say what would help you understand and participate.

sections.heading: Voluntary and involuntary care and your rights
paragraphs: Western Australia’s official guidance explains that involuntary treatment can take place in hospital or in the community. Ask about admission status and consent to each proposed treatment separately, rather than assuming that your status answers every question about treatment choices.

Each state and territory has its own mental health legislation, as the Australian Government explains: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. Ask the team: “What is my current legal status?”, “What does that mean for treatment and leaving hospital?” and “Which rules apply here?”

You can also ask: “How can I request a review?” and “Who can explain my rights independently?” In Western Australia, Think Mental Health’s laws and rights page describes the roles of the Mental Health Advocacy Service and Mental Health Tribunal: https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/.

In Victoria, the health department’s Act guide explains supported decision making and non-legal advocacy for people receiving compulsory mental health services: https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act. These resources describe their own jurisdictions, not nationwide rules. Elsewhere, ask staff for the relevant official health-department, tribunal or advocacy resource.

If the explanation is difficult to follow, you could say: “Please explain my status and choices in a language and format I understand. Can you arrange an interpreter or help me find suitable information?” Victoria’s official guide includes translated and easy-read resources. Ask what is available where you are.

sections.heading: A preparation checklist for you and your family
paragraphs: Follow the hospital’s own admission instructions rather than treating this as a universal packing list. Use these prompts to ask what you need and what can wait. Packing or paperwork should not delay urgent help: the Australian Government Department of Health advises going to your local hospital’s emergency department if you need urgent care.

Ask which documents and belongings to bring. Questions might include: “Do I need identification, Medicare or insurance details?” and “What clothing and toiletries are permitted?” Consider keeping important contact numbers somewhere you can access them without your phone. Confirm the hospital’s instructions before bringing items you are unsure about.

For health information, ask what the team needs about your current medicines, doses and allergies. If available, gather contact details for your treating clinicians and any existing care documents. Ask how to bring and hand over medicines, rather than assuming you should keep them with you or manage them yourself during admission.

Consider whether someone you trust could help with dependants, household tasks or contacting work or study. Discuss what you want that person to say and what you would prefer to keep private. If you need documentation for an absence, ask the hospital what it can provide and check what your workplace or education provider requires.

Check local arrangements for phones, chargers, valuables, visiting and any restrictions on belongings. Raise food needs, religious items or practices that matter to you, and ask what arrangements are possible.
Check with the hospital and, if applicable, your insurer whether there are any excess, gap or out-of-pocket charges.

sections.heading: Assessment, daily routines and treatment planning

subsections.heading: Assessment when you arrive
paragraphs: Ask the team to explain what your assessment will involve and what information they need from you. You could ask, “Who should I tell about my current concerns, physical health, medicines or anything that makes it difficult to feel safe?” If you need language or communication support, ask how this can be arranged for the assessment.
You can also raise what matters to you beyond your symptoms: “Could we discuss how my language, faith, previous experiences or family circumstances affect this plan?”

subsections.heading: Daily care and treatment decisions
paragraphs: Ask for an explanation of the ward’s daily arrangements, including meals, rest, any activities and opportunities to speak with the treating team. Confirm the rules about leave rather than relying on another person’s hospital experience. A useful starting question is, “Who can I speak to if I need help or have a concern between planned discussions?”

For treatment planning, ask who is coordinating your care, what each proposed treatment is intended to address, what alternatives exist and how your preferences will be considered. You can also ask the team to explain which decisions require your consent and how your current legal status affects those decisions.

If medicine is proposed, ask the prescriber or pharmacist about its purpose, expected benefits, possible side effects and when to seek help. Healthdirect’s medicines directory includes general information about antidepressants, antipsychotic medicines and lithium: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. Use it to prepare questions, not as individual prescribing advice or a reason to change your medicine yourself.

sections.heading: Ask for support that reflects your language and culture
paragraphs: Tell the team which language and dialect you prefer for conversations about your care. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ community mental health principles emphasise considering multicultural perspectives, but they do not establish what interpreter support a particular hospital offers.

Ask: “Could you arrange a qualified health interpreter in my preferred language and dialect for assessment, treatment discussions and discharge?” Follow up by asking what is available, how interpretation will happen and how confidentiality is handled.

If you would prefer not to have relatives interpret, you could say: “I would like to speak with the team without relatives interpreting. What arrangements are available?” Ask about a private conversation and what will happen if an interpreter is unavailable for a planned discussion. These are requests, not promises about a particular interpreter, appointment time or type of service.

Choose which parts of your identity and daily life you want the team to understand. That might include prayer, food needs, modesty, a preference about a clinician’s gender, or having no religious affiliation. Experiences of racism or concerns about stigma may also be relevant to what you want to discuss. You do not need to raise every topic, and someone from the same background may have different preferences.

You can ask: “How can we record what matters to me in my care plan, and revisit it if my needs change?” If fasting or another religious practice raises questions about treatment, ask the treating team to discuss it with you before making any changes to medicines.

sections.heading: How family can help while respecting privacy
paragraphs: Tell the treating team whom you would like involved, which conversations you want them to attend and what you would prefer to discuss privately. Your preferred support person might be a relative, chosen family member or trusted friend. Be specific about what feels helpful to you, rather than leaving others to assume that family members share your cultural, religious or treatment preferences.

You could say: “Please record who I want involved and what I am comfortable sharing. Can you explain when the law may allow or require information to be shared without my consent?” Ask how to update those preferences and what they mean in your circumstances.

Privacy preferences do not necessarily prevent every disclosure. For advice about consent, confidentiality exceptions or any formal carer or nominated-person role, ask the team to explain the applicable state or territory rules and provide the relevant official patient information.

If you are supporting someone in hospital, start by asking what they want from you. Check before visiting, offer help with responsibilities they agree to hand over, or write down questions they want to raise with the team. Listen without pressing them to explain more than they wish to share. Your perspective may be valuable, but it may differ from theirs.

If you have concerns to pass on, ask the team how to provide that information, how it will be recorded and who may see it. Also ask what the team can share with you in return. Do not assume that providing information means you will receive details about the person’s care, or that what you tell staff will remain confidential from them.

sections.heading: A discharge checklist for the next stage of care
paragraphs: Before you leave hospital, use these questions to discuss what happens next with your treating team. They are conversation prompts, not a standard discharge protocol or a promise that particular services or appointments will be available.

subsections.heading: Confirm follow-up and who is responsible
paragraphs: Ask: “Which appointments and referrals are confirmed, which still need arranging, and who is responsible for each?” Clarify whom to contact if an appointment is unavailable or you cannot attend.

Discuss how relevant information will reach your GP, community mental health team or therapist, and ask what consent arrangements apply. If something is still pending, ask what support you should use while waiting.

subsections.heading: Clarify medicines and prescription arrangements
paragraphs: If medicines are part of your plan, ask for a clear current list and an explanation of any changes. Questions for the prescriber or pharmacist include: “What is each medicine for? How should I take it? What side effects need attention, and whom should I contact?” Check how to obtain your supply and future prescriptions.

For general background, healthdirect’s medicines directory covers benefits, side effects and safe use of a range of medicines: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. It does not replace advice about your own prescription.

subsections.heading: Separate warning signs from emergency actions
paragraphs: Ask the team to discuss warning signs relevant to you and agree on what to do if they appear. Clarify which concerns should prompt contact with your treating service, which need urgent assessment, and what clinical contact is available after hours. Keep these details somewhere you can find them easily.

If someone is in immediate danger, call 000. Lifeline provides crisis support on 13 11 14 at any time, but this is not an emergency response service: https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114. For urgent care, go to your local hospital emergency department, as advised by the Australian Government Department of Health: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en.

subsections.heading: Carry your practical and cultural preferences forward
paragraphs: Discuss any work or study concerns, the support you would welcome from chosen family or friends, and what you want shared with them. Ask how interpreter needs and relevant cultural or religious preferences can be passed on to follow-up services. You might ask: “How will my next therapist understand my cultural context and coordinate with my treating team?”

sections.heading: Finding a community therapist who understands your context
paragraphs: For ongoing therapy after discharge, ask your treating team how a new therapist could fit into your care plan. Browsing profiles should not replace arranged psychiatric, medication or community follow-up, or be used to seek urgent care.

When speaking with a prospective therapist, start with what matters to you rather than feeling you need to explain your whole background. You might ask: “What experience do you have supporting people with my concerns?” and “How do you make room for culture, faith or language in therapy?” If relevant, ask whether you can use your preferred language and discuss family expectations or experiences of discrimination without assumptions about your community.

A shared background may be a meaningful preference, but it does not guarantee understanding or a good therapeutic fit. Questions such as “How do you work with someone whose background differs from yours?” and “What would you do if I felt misunderstood?” can help you discuss how the therapist approaches differences and responds to feedback. These are conversation prompts, not a validated way to assess a practitioner.

Before booking, ask about qualifications, experience with the support recommended at discharge, availability and fees. You can also ask: “With my consent, how would you coordinate with my GP or treating team, and what information would you share?” A profile is a starting point for that discussion, not confirmation that a practitioner can meet every post-hospital need.

sections.heading: Your next conversation with the care team
paragraphs: Before your next conversation with the care team, write down what you need explained, whom you would like involved and what support you need after discharge. Choose the concerns that matter to you, rather than feeling you have to cover everything at once.

Ask the team to clarify anything that remains uncertain, including who to contact about unanswered questions or gaps in follow-up. If you are considering a community therapist, ask how that support would fit alongside your agreed care plan.

summary_items.label: How can you request language and cultural support?
summary_items.description: Ask the hospital about a qualified health interpreter in your preferred language and dialect, and discuss personal needs such as prayer or food. Confirm what support is available and how preferences can be recorded.

summary_items.label: What should you clarify before leaving hospital?
summary_items.description: Ask your treating team to clarify follow-up appointments, medicine changes, personalised warning signs and after-hours contacts. Discuss how interpreter needs and relevant cultural preferences can be passed to follow-up services.

stack_native_entry.article_markdown: # What to Expect in a Mental Health Hospital in Australia Prepare for a mental health hospital stay in Australia with questions about admission, patient rights, cultural support, family involvement and discharge. ![A person in a dark sweater rests their chin on a fist, facing another person who gestures with a hand.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU0A4049LNR4%2FGshah810%2FTalaThrive-marketing-site%2Fimages%2Fhero-09482cca-8bed-423d-8ca5-7582a5560cbb.jpg?alt=media&token=acd60b69-8ca2-4fc2-bba0-0e2fd9ebd3bc) *Prepare for a mental health hospital stay in Australia with questions about admission, patient rights, cultural support, family involvement and discharge.* ## Quick Summary - **How can you request language and cultural support?:** Ask the hospital about a qualified health interpreter in your preferred language and dialect, and discuss personal needs such as prayer or food. Confirm what support is available and how preferences can be recorded. - **What should you clarify before leaving hospital?:** Ask your treating team to clarify follow-up appointments, medicine changes, personalised warning signs and after-hours contacts. Discuss how interpreter needs and relevant cultural preferences can be passed to follow-up services. ## What happens in a mental health hospital? If someone is in immediate danger, call 000, as Lifeline advises. For urgent care, the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing directs people to their local hospital emergency department. Lifeline also provides crisis support on 13 11 14, available 24/7. If a mental health hospital admission is being considered, ask the team to explain what assessment will involve, how treatment decisions will be made and how they will plan for care after you leave. Confirm the arrangements at the hospital involved rather than expecting a fixed routine, length of stay or outcome. You may also have questions about speaking in your preferred language, involving family, managing work or keeping information private. You can raise these alongside questions about treatment and explain which concerns matter most to you. Browsing community therapist profiles is a separate option for routine support, not a way to obtain urgent care or hospital admission. ## How admission can happen If you need urgent care, go to the emergency department at your local hospital. The Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing also lists your state or territory’s Mental Health Crisis Assessment and Treatment Team as a source of help. Its mental health overview provides these urgent-help routes, rather than a complete guide to admission: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. For a possible planned admission, ask your GP, psychiatrist or current treating service who to contact and what the local process involves. Useful questions include: “What referral or assessment is needed?”, “Who decides whether inpatient care is appropriate?” and “What happens if admission is not recommended or a bed is unavailable?” Ask the hospital to explain its requirements rather than treating a referral as confirmation of a place. If you are considering private care, ask the hospital and your insurer separately about cover and potential costs. You can raise communication needs before arriving: “Can my preferred language, dialect or accessibility needs be recorded?” and “How can I request a qualified interpreter for the assessment?” You do not need to wait until a treatment discussion to say what would help you understand and participate. ![Back view of a person in a dark quilted jacket with a shoulder strap, near glass doors and a wheeled stretcher.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU0A4049LNR4%2FGshah810%2FTalaThrive-marketing-site%2Fimages%2Finline-2a483aaa-5812-4051-88c1-1cca679d8035.jpg?alt=media&token=f982cbeb-0323-4aa5-8e2f-67e509eb5ca3) ## Voluntary and involuntary care and your rights Western Australia’s official guidance explains that involuntary treatment can take place in hospital or in the community. Ask about admission status and consent to each proposed treatment separately, rather than assuming that your status answers every question about treatment choices. Each state and territory has its own mental health legislation, as the Australian Government explains: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. Ask the team: “What is my current legal status?”, “What does that mean for treatment and leaving hospital?” and “Which rules apply here?” You can also ask: “How can I request a review?” and “Who can explain my rights independently?” In Western Australia, Think Mental Health’s laws and rights page describes the roles of the Mental Health Advocacy Service and Mental Health Tribunal: https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/. In Victoria, the health department’s Act guide explains supported decision making and non-legal advocacy for people receiving compulsory mental health services: https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act. These resources describe their own jurisdictions, not nationwide rules. Elsewhere, ask staff for the relevant official health-department, tribunal or advocacy resource. If the explanation is difficult to follow, you could say: “Please explain my status and choices in a language and format I understand. Can you arrange an interpreter or help me find suitable information?” Victoria’s official guide includes translated and easy-read resources. Ask what is available where you are. > **Check the rules that apply to you** > > Ask staff to explain which state or territory rules apply to your circumstances. This guide is not individual legal advice. ## A preparation checklist for you and your family Follow the hospital’s own admission instructions rather than treating this as a universal packing list. Use these prompts to ask what you need and what can wait. Packing or paperwork should not delay urgent help: the Australian Government Department of Health advises going to your local hospital’s emergency department if you need urgent care. Ask which documents and belongings to bring. Questions might include: “Do I need identification, Medicare or insurance details?” and “What clothing and toiletries are permitted?” Consider keeping important contact numbers somewhere you can access them without your phone. Confirm the hospital’s instructions before bringing items you are unsure about. For health information, ask what the team needs about your current medicines, doses and allergies. If available, gather contact details for your treating clinicians and any existing care documents. Ask how to bring and hand over medicines, rather than assuming you should keep them with you or manage them yourself during admission. Consider whether someone you trust could help with dependants, household tasks or contacting work or study. Discuss what you want that person to say and what you would prefer to keep private. If you need documentation for an absence, ask the hospital what it can provide and check what your workplace or education provider requires. Check local arrangements for phones, chargers, valuables, visiting and any restrictions on belongings. Raise food needs, religious items or practices that matter to you, and ask what arrangements are possible. Check with the hospital and, if applicable, your insurer whether there are any excess, gap or out-of-pocket charges. ## Assessment, daily routines and treatment planning ### Assessment when you arrive Ask the team to explain what your assessment will involve and what information they need from you. You could ask, “Who should I tell about my current concerns, physical health, medicines or anything that makes it difficult to feel safe?” If you need language or communication support, ask how this can be arranged for the assessment. You can also raise what matters to you beyond your symptoms: “Could we discuss how my language, faith, previous experiences or family circumstances affect this plan?” ### Daily care and treatment decisions Ask for an explanation of the ward’s daily arrangements, including meals, rest, any activities and opportunities to speak with the treating team. Confirm the rules about leave rather than relying on another person’s hospital experience. A useful starting question is, “Who can I speak to if I need help or have a concern between planned discussions?” For treatment planning, ask who is coordinating your care, what each proposed treatment is intended to address, what alternatives exist and how your preferences will be considered. You can also ask the team to explain which decisions require your consent and how your current legal status affects those decisions. If medicine is proposed, ask the prescriber or pharmacist about its purpose, expected benefits, possible side effects and when to seek help. Healthdirect’s medicines directory includes general information about antidepressants, antipsychotic medicines and lithium: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. Use it to prepare questions, not as individual prescribing advice or a reason to change your medicine yourself. ## Ask for support that reflects your language and culture Tell the team which language and dialect you prefer for conversations about your care. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ community mental health principles emphasise considering multicultural perspectives, but they do not establish what interpreter support a particular hospital offers. Ask: “Could you arrange a qualified health interpreter in my preferred language and dialect for assessment, treatment discussions and discharge?” Follow up by asking what is available, how interpretation will happen and how confidentiality is handled. If you would prefer not to have relatives interpret, you could say: “I would like to speak with the team without relatives interpreting. What arrangements are available?” Ask about a private conversation and what will happen if an interpreter is unavailable for a planned discussion. These are requests, not promises about a particular interpreter, appointment time or type of service. Choose which parts of your identity and daily life you want the team to understand. That might include prayer, food needs, modesty, a preference about a clinician’s gender, or having no religious affiliation. Experiences of racism or concerns about stigma may also be relevant to what you want to discuss. You do not need to raise every topic, and someone from the same background may have different preferences. You can ask: “How can we record what matters to me in my care plan, and revisit it if my needs change?” If fasting or another religious practice raises questions about treatment, ask the treating team to discuss it with you before making any changes to medicines. ## How family can help while respecting privacy Tell the treating team whom you would like involved, which conversations you want them to attend and what you would prefer to discuss privately. Your preferred support person might be a relative, chosen family member or trusted friend. Be specific about what feels helpful to you, rather than leaving others to assume that family members share your cultural, religious or treatment preferences. You could say: “Please record who I want involved and what I am comfortable sharing. Can you explain when the law may allow or require information to be shared without my consent?” Ask how to update those preferences and what they mean in your circumstances. Privacy preferences do not necessarily prevent every disclosure. For advice about consent, confidentiality exceptions or any formal carer or nominated-person role, ask the team to explain the applicable state or territory rules and provide the relevant official patient information. If you are supporting someone in hospital, start by asking what they want from you. Check before visiting, offer help with responsibilities they agree to hand over, or write down questions they want to raise with the team. Listen without pressing them to explain more than they wish to share. Your perspective may be valuable, but it may differ from theirs. If you have concerns to pass on, ask the team how to provide that information, how it will be recorded and who may see it. Also ask what the team can share with you in return. Do not assume that providing information means you will receive details about the person’s care, or that what you tell staff will remain confidential from them. ## A discharge checklist for the next stage of care Before you leave hospital, use these questions to discuss what happens next with your treating team. They are conversation prompts, not a standard discharge protocol or a promise that particular services or appointments will be available. ### Confirm follow-up and who is responsible Ask: “Which appointments and referrals are confirmed, which still need arranging, and who is responsible for each?” Clarify whom to contact if an appointment is unavailable or you cannot attend. Discuss how relevant information will reach your GP, community mental health team or therapist, and ask what consent arrangements apply. If something is still pending, ask what support you should use while waiting. ### Clarify medicines and prescription arrangements If medicines are part of your plan, ask for a clear current list and an explanation of any changes. Questions for the prescriber or pharmacist include: “What is each medicine for? How should I take it? What side effects need attention, and whom should I contact?” Check how to obtain your supply and future prescriptions. For general background, healthdirect’s medicines directory covers benefits, side effects and safe use of a range of medicines: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. It does not replace advice about your own prescription. ### Separate warning signs from emergency actions Ask the team to discuss warning signs relevant to you and agree on what to do if they appear. Clarify which concerns should prompt contact with your treating service, which need urgent assessment, and what clinical contact is available after hours. Keep these details somewhere you can find them easily. If someone is in immediate danger, call 000. Lifeline provides crisis support on 13 11 14 at any time, but this is not an emergency response service: https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114. For urgent care, go to your local hospital emergency department, as advised by the Australian Government Department of Health: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. ### Carry your practical and cultural preferences forward Discuss any work or study concerns, the support you would welcome from chosen family or friends, and what you want shared with them. Ask how interpreter needs and relevant cultural or religious preferences can be passed on to follow-up services. You might ask: “How will my next therapist understand my cultural context and coordinate with my treating team?” ## Finding a community therapist who understands your context For ongoing therapy after discharge, ask your treating team how a new therapist could fit into your care plan. Browsing profiles should not replace arranged psychiatric, medication or community follow-up, or be used to seek urgent care. When speaking with a prospective therapist, start with what matters to you rather than feeling you need to explain your whole background. You might ask: “What experience do you have supporting people with my concerns?” and “How do you make room for culture, faith or language in therapy?” If relevant, ask whether you can use your preferred language and discuss family expectations or experiences of discrimination without assumptions about your community. A shared background may be a meaningful preference, but it does not guarantee understanding or a good therapeutic fit. Questions such as “How do you work with someone whose background differs from yours?” and “What would you do if I felt misunderstood?” can help you discuss how the therapist approaches differences and responds to feedback. These are conversation prompts, not a validated way to assess a practitioner. Before booking, ask about qualifications, experience with the support recommended at discharge, availability and fees. You can also ask: “With my consent, how would you coordinate with my GP or treating team, and what information would you share?” A profile is a starting point for that discussion, not confirmation that a practitioner can meet every post-hospital need. ## Your next conversation with the care team Before your next conversation with the care team, write down what you need explained, whom you would like involved and what support you need after discharge. Choose the concerns that matter to you, rather than feeling you have to cover everything at once. Ask the team to clarify anything that remains uncertain, including who to contact about unanswered questions or gaps in follow-up. If you are considering a community therapist, ask how that support would fit alongside your agreed care plan. ![A mug, pen, spiral notebook and closed laptop sit on a wooden table near a window, with leafy plants and a wooden chair nearby.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU0A4049LNR4%2FGshah810%2FTalaThrive-marketing-site%2Fimages%2Finline-fb769e4f-74ad-4e48-a62c-17c5e4addd69.jpg?alt=media&token=c079322d-268f-4e67-b893-6551367552a2) ## Next Step **Sign up** Browse therapists that match your cultural background [Browse therapists that understand your cultural background](https://app.talathrive.com/login) ## References - [Lifeline crisis support - 13 11 14](https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114) - [Medicines information | healthdirect](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines) - [What we're doing about mental health | Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en) - [Mental health for the community | RANZCP](https://www.ranzcp.org/clinical-guidelines-publications/clinical-guidelines-publications-library/mental-health-for-the-community) - [Mental Health and Wellbeing Act 2022 | health.vic.gov.au](https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act) - [Mental Health Laws And Rights | Think Mental Health](https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/) - [Bruce Private Hospital | Hyson Green mental health | Calvary Health Care](https://www.calvarycare.org.au/hospitals/calvary-bruce-private-hospital/services-and-clinics-1/hyson-green-mental-health) - [Tala Thrive | Culturally matched therapy & coaching](https://talathrive.com/)

Tell the treating team whom you would like involved, which conversations you want them to attend and what you would prefer to discuss privately. Your preferred support person might be a relative, chosen family member or trusted friend. Be specific about what feels helpful to you, rather than leaving others to assume that family members share your cultural, religious or treatment preferences.

You could say: “Please record who I want involved and what I am comfortable sharing. Can you explain when the law may allow or require information to be shared without my consent?” Ask how to update those preferences and what they mean in your circumstances.

Privacy preferences do not necessarily prevent every disclosure. For advice about consent, confidentiality exceptions or any formal carer or nominated-person role, ask the team to explain the applicable state or territory rules and provide the relevant official patient information.

If you are supporting someone in hospital, start by asking what they want from you. Check before visiting, offer help with responsibilities they agree to hand over, or write down questions they want to raise with the team. Listen without pressing them to explain more than they wish to share. Your perspective may be valuable, but it may differ from theirs.

If you have concerns to pass on, ask the team how to provide that information, how it will be recorded and who may see it. Also ask what the team can share with you in return. Do not assume that providing information means you will receive details about the person’s care, or that what you tell staff will remain confidential from them.

A discharge checklist for the next stage of care

Before you leave hospital, use these questions to discuss what happens next with your treating team. They are conversation prompts, not a standard discharge protocol or a promise that particular services or appointments will be available.

Confirm follow-up and who is responsible

Ask: “Which appointments and referrals are confirmed, which still need arranging, and who is responsible for each?” Clarify whom to contact if an appointment is unavailable or you cannot attend.

Discuss how relevant information will reach your GP, community mental health team or therapist, and ask what consent arrangements apply. If something is still pending, ask what support you should use while waiting.

Clarify medicines and prescription arrangements

If medicines are part of your plan, ask for a clear current list and an explanation of any changes. Questions for the prescriber or pharmacist include: “What is each medicine for? How should I take it? What side effects need attention, and whom should I contact?” Check how to obtain your supply and future prescriptions.

For general background, healthdirect’s medicines directory covers benefits, side effects and safe use of a range of medicines: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. It does not replace advice about your own prescription.

Separate warning signs from emergency actions

Ask the team to discuss warning signs relevant to you and agree on what to do if they appear. Clarify which concerns should prompt contact with your treating service, which need urgent assessment, and what clinical contact is available after hours. Keep these details somewhere you can find them easily.

If someone is in immediate danger, call 000. Lifeline provides crisis support on 13 11 14 at any time, but this is not an emergency response service: https://www.lifeline.org.au/131114. For urgent care, go to your local hospital emergency department, as advised by the Australian Government Department of Health: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en.

Carry your practical and cultural preferences forward

Discuss any work or study concerns, the support you would welcome from chosen family or friends, and what you want shared with them. Ask how interpreter needs and relevant cultural or religious preferences can be passed on to follow-up services. You might ask: “How will my next therapist understand my cultural context and coordinate with my treating team?”

Finding a community therapist who understands your context

For ongoing therapy after discharge, ask your treating team how a new therapist could fit into your care plan. Browsing profiles should not replace arranged psychiatric, medication or community follow-up, or be used to seek urgent care.

When speaking with a prospective therapist, start with what matters to you rather than feeling you need to explain your whole background. You might ask: “What experience do you have supporting people with my concerns?” and “How do you make room for culture, faith or language in therapy?” If relevant, ask whether you can use your preferred language and discuss family expectations or experiences of discrimination without assumptions about your community.

A shared background may be a meaningful preference, but it does not guarantee understanding or a good therapeutic fit. Questions such as “How do you work with someone whose background differs from yours?” and “What would you do if I felt misunderstood?” can help you discuss how the therapist approaches differences and responds to feedback. These are conversation prompts, not a validated way to assess a practitioner.

Before booking, ask about qualifications, experience with the support recommended at discharge, availability and fees. You can also ask: “With my consent, how would you coordinate with my GP or treating team, and what information would you share?” A profile is a starting point for that discussion, not confirmation that a practitioner can meet every post-hospital need.

Your next conversation with the care team

Before your next conversation with the care team, write down what you need explained, whom you would like involved and what support you need after discharge. Choose the concerns that matter to you, rather than feeling you have to cover everything at once.

Ask the team to clarify anything that remains uncertain, including who to contact about unanswered questions or gaps in follow-up. If you are considering a community therapist, ask how that support would fit alongside your agreed care plan.

sections.heading: What happens in a mental health hospital?
paragraphs: If someone is in immediate danger, call 000, as Lifeline advises. For urgent care, the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing directs people to their local hospital emergency department. Lifeline also provides crisis support on 13 11 14, available 24/7.

If a mental health hospital admission is being considered, ask the team to explain what assessment will involve, how treatment decisions will be made and how they will plan for care after you leave. Confirm the arrangements at the hospital involved rather than expecting a fixed routine, length of stay or outcome.

You may also have questions about speaking in your preferred language, involving family, managing work or keeping information private. You can raise these alongside questions about treatment and explain which concerns matter most to you. Browsing community therapist profiles is a separate option for routine support, not a way to obtain urgent care or hospital admission.

sections.heading: How admission can happen
paragraphs: If you need urgent care, go to the emergency department at your local hospital. The Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing also lists your state or territory’s Mental Health Crisis Assessment and Treatment Team as a source of help. Its mental health overview provides these urgent-help routes, rather than a complete guide to admission: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en.

For a possible planned admission, ask your GP, psychiatrist or current treating service who to contact and what the local process involves. Useful questions include: “What referral or assessment is needed?”, “Who decides whether inpatient care is appropriate?” and “What happens if admission is not recommended or a bed is unavailable?”

Ask the hospital to explain its requirements rather than treating a referral as confirmation of a place. If you are considering private care, ask the hospital and your insurer separately about cover and potential costs.

You can raise communication needs before arriving: “Can my preferred language, dialect or accessibility needs be recorded?” and “How can I request a qualified interpreter for the assessment?” You do not need to wait until a treatment discussion to say what would help you understand and participate.

sections.heading: Voluntary and involuntary care and your rights
paragraphs: Western Australia’s official guidance explains that involuntary treatment can take place in hospital or in the community. Ask about admission status and consent to each proposed treatment separately, rather than assuming that your status answers every question about treatment choices.

Each state and territory has its own mental health legislation, as the Australian Government explains: https://www.health.gov.au/topics/mental-health-and-suicide-prevention/what-were-doing-about-mental-health?language=en. Ask the team: “What is my current legal status?”, “What does that mean for treatment and leaving hospital?” and “Which rules apply here?”

You can also ask: “How can I request a review?” and “Who can explain my rights independently?” In Western Australia, Think Mental Health’s laws and rights page describes the roles of the Mental Health Advocacy Service and Mental Health Tribunal: https://www.thinkmentalhealthwa.com.au/mental-health-support-services/mental-health-laws-and-rights/.

In Victoria, the health department’s Act guide explains supported decision making and non-legal advocacy for people receiving compulsory mental health services: https://www.health.vic.gov.au/mental-health-and-wellbeing-act. These resources describe their own jurisdictions, not nationwide rules. Elsewhere, ask staff for the relevant official health-department, tribunal or advocacy resource.

If the explanation is difficult to follow, you could say: “Please explain my status and choices in a language and format I understand. Can you arrange an interpreter or help me find suitable information?” Victoria’s official guide includes translated and easy-read resources. Ask what is available where you are.

sections.heading: A preparation checklist for you and your family
paragraphs: Follow the hospital’s own admission instructions rather than treating this as a universal packing list. Use these prompts to ask what you need and what can wait. Packing or paperwork should not delay urgent help: the Australian Government Department of Health advises going to your local hospital’s emergency department if you need urgent care.

Ask which documents and belongings to bring. Questions might include: “Do I need identification, Medicare or insurance details?” and “What clothing and toiletries are permitted?” Consider keeping important contact numbers somewhere you can access them without your phone. Confirm the hospital’s instructions before bringing items you are unsure about.

For health information, ask what the team needs about your current medicines, doses and allergies. If available, gather contact details for your treating clinicians and any existing care documents. Ask how to bring and hand over medicines, rather than assuming you should keep them with you or manage them yourself during admission.

Consider whether someone you trust could help with dependants, household tasks or contacting work or study. Discuss what you want that person to say and what you would prefer to keep private. If you need documentation for an absence, ask the hospital what it can provide and check what your workplace or education provider requires.

Check local arrangements for phones, chargers, valuables, visiting and any restrictions on belongings. Raise food needs, religious items or practices that matter to you, and ask what arrangements are possible.
Check with the hospital and, if applicable, your insurer whether there are any excess, gap or out-of-pocket charges.

sections.heading: Assessment, daily routines and treatment planning

subsections.heading: Assessment when you arrive
paragraphs: Ask the team to explain what your assessment will involve and what information they need from you. You could ask, “Who should I tell about my current concerns, physical health, medicines or anything that makes it difficult to feel safe?” If you need language or communication support, ask how this can be arranged for the assessment.
You can also raise what matters to you beyond your symptoms: “Could we discuss how my language, faith, previous experiences or family circumstances affect this plan?”

subsections.heading: Daily care and treatment decisions
paragraphs: Ask for an explanation of the ward’s daily arrangements, including meals, rest, any activities and opportunities to speak with the treating team. Confirm the rules about leave rather than relying on another person’s hospital experience. A useful starting question is, “Who can I speak to if I need help or have a concern between planned discussions?”

For treatment planning, ask who is coordinating your care, what each proposed treatment is intended to address, what alternatives exist and how your preferences will be considered. You can also ask the team to explain which decisions require your consent and how your current legal status affects those decisions.

If medicine is proposed, ask the prescriber or pharmacist about its purpose, expected benefits, possible side effects and when to seek help. Healthdirect’s medicines directory includes general information about antidepressants, antipsychotic medicines and lithium: https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/medicines. Use it to prepare questions, not as individual prescribing advice or a reason to change your medicine yourself.

sections.heading: Ask for support that reflects your language and culture
paragraphs: Tell the team which language and dialect you prefer for conversations about your care. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists’ community mental health principles emphasise considering multicultural perspectives, but they do not establish what interpreter support a particular hospital offers.

Ask: “Could you arrange a qualified health interpreter in my preferred language and dialect for assessment, treatment discussions and discharge?” Follow up by asking what is available, how interpretation will happen and how confidentiality is handled.

If you would prefer not to have relatives interpret, you could say: “I would like to speak with the team without relatives interpreting. What arrangements are available?” Ask about a private conversation and what will happen if an interpreter is unavailable for a planned discussion. These are requests, not promises about a particular interpreter, appointment time or type of service.

Choose which parts of your identity and daily life you want the team to understand. That might include prayer, food needs, modesty, a preference about a clinician’s gender, or having no religious affiliation. Experiences of racism or concerns about stigma may also be relevant to what you want to discuss. You do not need to raise every topic, and someone from the same background may have different preferences.

You can ask: “How can we record what matters to me in my care plan, and revisit it if my needs change?” If fasting or another religious practice raises questions about treatment, ask the treating team to discuss it with you before making any changes to medicines.
